Shafali leads India to 149/6 against Bangladesh
item.description:
Shafali Verma made the most of three dropped catches to smash a 40-ball 64 as India posted 149 for 6 against Bangladesh in the Women’s Asia Cup semi-final in Dubai on Thursday.

Bangladesh, who won the toss and opted to field, were made to pay for their lapses in the field as Shafali struck seven fours and three sixes.

Shafali was given her first reprieve in the second over when Fahima Khatun failed to hold on to a difficult catch at long-on off Sultana Khatun. Two overs later, Nahida Akter dropped another low chance at mid-on off Marufa Akter.

India reach 45/1 in powerplay as Bangladesh drop Shafali twice

Shafali was also involved in a failed run-out opportunity before Bangladesh finally ended her innings in the 14th over. Sultana Khatun took the catch through substitute fielder Farjana Easmin to dismiss the opener for 64 off 40 balls.

Shafali had put India in control after the early dismissal of Smriti Mandhana, who was caught by Shorna Akter off Sultana for just two.

She then added 50 runs off 44 balls with Pratika Rawal. Rawal was dismissed for 20 off 24 balls in the 10th over, with Dilara Akter taking the catch off Rabeya Khan.

India were 45 for 1 at the end of the powerplay, but Shafali’s aggressive batting helped them build momentum in the middle overs.

After Shafali’s dismissal, Harmanpreet Kaur and Richa Ghosh added valuable runs. Harmanpreet remained unbeaten on 24 off 28 balls, hitting two sixes, while Richa scored 21 off 16 balls with two sixes.

Deepti Sharma provided a late boost with a six and a four in her 13 off six balls before Rabeya Khan caught her off Marufa Akter in the final over.
Marufa and Sultana Khatun took one and two wickets respectively, while Nahida and Rabeya claimed one each.

India eventually finished on 149 for 6 after 20 overs, leaving Bangladesh with a target of 150 to reach the final.

item.title: Indian traders seek Bangladeshi hilsa for Durga Puja, which companies want to export
item.description:
Eighteen Bangladeshi companies have applied for permission to export hilsa to India ahead of Durga Puja. At the same time, the Fish Importers Association of India has sought permission to import hilsa from Bangladesh.

The Ministry of Commerce has sought the opinion of the Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock to determine whether permission should be granted for the exports, according to sources at the Ministry of Commerce.

After receiving the applications from exporters, the Ministry of Commerce sent a letter to the Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock yesterday, Wednesday, seeking its opinion on the supply and demand situation of hilsa in the country.

A decision on whether to allow hilsa exports to India will be made based on that opinion.

Last year, the Bangladesh government allowed the export of 1,200 tonnes of hilsa to India, but only 150 tonnes were eventually exported.

Commerce Secretary Md Ataur Rahman Khan told Prothom Alo, “A decision on the permission will be made soon after receiving the opinion from the Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock. I hope we receive a positive opinion in favour of allowing the exports.”

This year, Bangladeshi exporters have sought permission to export hilsa for a longer period instead of the short period allowed in previous years. They have requested permission for at least two months, and preferably throughout the year.

Traders argue that it becomes difficult to complete opening letters of credit (LCs), collecting hilsa, processing and packaging within just 20 to 25 days.

Companies interested in exporting hilsa

The companies that have sought permission this year include Bishwas Enterprise of Khulna; JS Enterprise and Anraj Fish Products of Chattogram; Lucky Enterprise, MUC Foods, Mohtab & Sons and Janata Fish of Jashore; Vigilant Express, Swarnali Enterprise, Majestic Enterprise and BDS Corporation of Dhaka; Mahima Enterprise, AR Enterprise and Tanisha Enterprise of Barishal; Rafid Enterprise of Bhola; and MA Enterprise and Suman Traders of Satkhira.

The Fish Importers Association of India has sought permission to import hilsa from Bangladesh. The organisation recently sent separate letters to the Prime Minister’s Office, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Ministry of Commerce, making the request.

Urging that permission for exports be granted by mid-September, the Indian trade body said Bangladesh used to export an average of around 5,000 tonnes of hilsa to India every year since 1996.

Although exports continued intermittently, hilsa exports resumed in September 2019 with special permission for a limited period on the occasion of Durga Puja.

Exports lower than permitted

According to sources at the Ministry of Commerce, hilsa exports to India have consistently been lower than the quantities permitted.

After a long hiatus, permission was given to export 500 tonnes of hilsa in 2019, while 1,850 tonnes were approved for export in 2020. In 2021, against permission to export 4,600 tonnes, 1,200 tonnes were exported.

In 2022, 1,300 tonnes were exported against permission for 2,900 tonnes. In 2023, permission was given for 3,950 tonnes, but 1,300 tonnes were exported.

And in 2024, only 577 tonnes of hilsa were exported to India against approval to export 2,420 tonnes.

item.title: Apple joins foldable phone race with $1,999 passport-shaped iPhone Duo
item.description:
APPLE-EVENT/SAMSUNG

  • Duo opens to 7.6-inch screen, uses Apple's A20 Pro chip, starts at $1,999.

  • iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max prices start at $1,199 and $1,299.

  • New AirPods start at $129 with noise cancellation for budget line.

Apple on Wednesday redefined its flagship smartphone with the launch of the Duo, a folding USD 1,999 iPhone, betting its design and promises of data privacy will let it leap ahead of rivals who have been selling folding phones for years.

The Duo could shake up a category long dominated by Samsung and Chinese companies like Huawei, whose devices have struggled to move beyond a niche audience. Analysts have long said Apple's entry could be the catalyst foldables need, helping bring the form factor into the mainstream much as the company did with smartwatches and wireless earbuds.

The Duo is sized and shaped like a passport, with rounded edges. It opens into a horizontal, 7.6-inch-diagonal (19 cm) screen that also can be viewed vertically. There is a smaller single screen on the front, when the phone is folded. When open, it is Apple's thinnest phone, the company said. However, it is thicker than folding phones offered by Chinese rivals.

New CEO John Ternus led the event, for the most notable overhaul of Apple's flagship product since the iPhone X in 2017. The iPhone brought in USD 209.6 billion, or just over half of Apple's sales, in its most recent fiscal year.

Ternus criticised existing foldables as awkward and poorly suited for common tasks such as scrolling and video viewing, saying the Duo was designed to deliver an iPad-like experience in a pocket-sized device through a custom hinge, dual displays with a consistent aspect ratio, and a new titanium body.

"It's entirely new and at the same time remarkably familiar. A similar size to your passport, it feels familiar to hold and comfortable to use with one hand," Ternus said.

Other tech companies made light of the launch. Duolingo, the foreign-language learning app with a green owl mascot named Duo, messaged on X, "We infringed upon," with laughing-crying emojis. That drew a message of "solidarity" from foldable phone company Samsung Mobile US, which added, "They copied us, too."

Analysts predict strong market share

It will fall to Ternus, the previously low-profile hardware chief, to persuade Apple's customers that they need a foldable device costing about USD 2,000, a new high for a global brand that has defined mass luxury. Analyst firms such as International Data Corporation expect Apple will sell every foldable iPhone it can produce and secure a 40 per cent share of the lucrative niche by the end of next year.

Apple positioned the iPhone Duo as a business productivity device, showing how it would manage Zoom calls with multiple participants and a broader view of the Slack messaging app. The Duo's larger screen will support multiple app windows at once, a move aimed at productivity that Apple has made with some of its iPads.

Apple said the iPhone Duo, available from 23 October, will feature the A20 Pro chip to drive its displays and also a new C2 modem chip designed by Apple, part of its move away from Qualcomm's wireless data chips. Its battery supports 24 hours of mixed dual-screen use and can charge to 50 per cent in about 20 minutes.

"Apple showed up years after everyone else, yet it walks in and sets the rules. Apple entered the foldable market and, in one keynote, set the price and the standard every rival will now be measured against," said Francisco Jeronimo, vice president for Data and Analytics, Devices, at IDC EMEA.

"The real fight is China, where Huawei owns nearly 80 per cent of foldables. Apple has just given Chinese buyers a reason to look up. Huawei owns China's foldable market today. Apple has just handed Chinese buyers their first genuinely compelling reason to reconsider."

Samsung has launched a publicity campaign for its foldable phones, as it seeks to defend its leadership in the segment, which it pioneered in 2019.

“Apple’s entry is a serious threat to Samsung, particularly in North America," said Paolo Pescatore, founder of research firm PP Foresight, adding Samsung for the first time faced a competitor capable of taking the category mainstream.

Apple shares closed down 0.3 per cent at USD 315.34 on Wednesday, following the presentation.

New CEO Ternus Highlights Privacy in AI

Former CEO Tim Cook handed off to Ternus at the start of the presentation with a video of a joking debate about how to begin the event. The video closed with a closeup of Cook, who said, "Not me. That's your guy," pointing back toward the new CEO.

Ternus described the iPhone platform as a personal AI hub that focused on privacy, saying that others wanted to collect and store personal data. "Honestly, trust only goes so far when your data is no longer yours to control," he said. "That's why Apple Intelligence runs on device whenever it can."

Apple's Lilian Rincon, who oversees AI products for the iPhone maker and was recruited from Google earlier this year, described an updated Siri assistant.

Executives also showed off the iPhone 18 Pro and the 18 Pro Max handsets that are the latest versions of Apple's well-known line, which do not fold. Pricing for the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max starts at USD 1,199 and USD 1,299, up USD 100 from the starting prices of the iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max.

AirPods and Apple Watch Updates

Apple also unveiled a feature aimed at addressing growing concerns over AI-generated and manipulated images. It introduced a new standard it calls "Apple Reference Image" to prove the authenticity of the images taken with the new iPhone 18 Pro cameras and said it will also support the emerging SynthID standard for identifying images that have been created or edited with AI. The Apple Reference Image feature will not be available in the EU or China.

The iPhone 18 Pro also will include the new A20 Pro chip, which brings improvements to help advanced AI models run directly on iPhones.

The company also said a new version of AirPods would start at USD 129 with noise cancellation, a first for its budget line of earbuds. Apple also unveiled the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4, positioned as major health-focused upgrades with new features that gauge recovery and fitness, as well as improved heart-rate tracking.

Micron CEO Sanjay Mehrotra attended the launch, notable because Apple rarely gives suppliers a prominent role at such events. As Apple adds more AI features to iPhones and other products, demand for high-performance memory has increased, elevating the strategic role of suppliers such as Micron, especially amid a global shortage of memory chips.

item.title: India reach 45/1 in powerplay as Bangladesh drop Shafali twice
item.description:
India reached 45 for 1 in the powerplay against Bangladesh in the Women’s Asia Cup semifinal in Dubai on Thursday, with Shafali Verma surviving two dropped catches in the opening three overs.

Shafali made 29 off 18 balls, hitting two fours and two sixes, while Pratika Rawal scored 14 off 13 balls as India made a brisk start after Bangladesh won the toss and opted to field.

Bangladesh had an early chance to dismiss Shafali when Fahima Khatun failed to hold on to a difficult catch at long-on off Sultana Khatun’s bowling. Shafali was given another reprieve soon after when Nahida Akter could not complete a low catch at mid-on off Marufa Akter.

Bangladesh did, however, claim the wicket of Smriti Mandhana, with Sworna Akter taking the catch.

Bangladesh have won only three of their 24 T20Is against India, with two of those victories coming when they restricted India to below 110. They will now look to contain India in the remainder of the semifinal and secure a place in the Asia Cup final.

item.title: Nepal seeks survivors two weeks after deadly floods
item.description:
Nepali rescuers clung to hopes of finding survivors trapped in hydropower tunnels on Wednesday, two weeks after deadly flooding triggered by a glacial mountain collapse.
The August 26 tsunami-like surge of water, mud and debris, which began on the China-Nepal border, has killed more than 1,410 people and left 5,651 missing.
“The rescue and search work in the tunnels at Trishuli 3A, 3B and Chilime hydropower projects is ongoing,” Nepal Army spokesman Raja Ram Basnet told AFP.
In Nepal, 1,367 bodies have been recovered and 5,132 people are missing, its disaster authority said on Wednesday.
In China, 43 people are dead and 519 are missing, according to state media.
Hundreds of foreigners are among the missing, as well as hundreds of hydropower workers.
Three people were rescued from deep inside tunnels -- two Nepalis on Friday and a Chinese man on Saturday.
But there has been no official confirmation of further survivors since then.
Authorities appealed on Wednesday for overseas family members of the missing -- preferably parents or children -- to submit DNA samples via email.
A public notice outlined specific types of genetic tests the family members should seek out depending on their sex and relationship to the missing person.
Thousands of people displaced by the disaster are living in camps, and the charity Save the Children said as many as 540 children had been separated from their parents.
Nepal police said they were taking extra care to ensure the safety of children and women in relief camps.
“We have become more vigilant in temporary holding centers in the affected areas where there are children, women or minority groups who could be victims of sexual abuse,” said Nepal Police spokesman Abi Narayan Kafle.
“We have also started providing psychosocial counselling in different camps,” he told AFP.
While the exact cause of the glacial collapse is unclear, climate change is accelerating glacial melt worldwide and increasing the risk of such disasters.
Nepal, a largely rural nation of 30 million people that has contributed little to the greenhouse gas emissions driving global warming, has said reconstruction could cost billions of dollars.
Kafle said security personnel have involved community members to search for bodies feared buried under debris.
“We have started a special search campaign for missing bodies all across the Bhotekoshi river corridor,” he said.
“We are also using drones to search for bodies.”

item.title: IAB announces protests against Property Transfer Act
item.description:
Islami Andolan Bangladesh (IAB) has called for further review and amendments to the recently passed Property Transfer (Amendment) Act, saying it could conflict with Islamic Shariah provisions on inheritance.
IAB Senior Nayeb-e-Ameer Mufti Syed Muhammad Faizul Karim announced rallies and processions in all divisional cities on September 11 to protest the passage of the law.
He made the announcement at a press conference at the IAB auditorium in Purana Paltan, Dhaka, on Thursday.
In a written statement, Faizul Karim said Shariah contains detailed provisions governing property transfer and inheritance, warning that the new law could allow property to be registered in children’s names while bypassing Shariah rules.
He acknowledged social problems such as parents being deprived of property or evicted from their homes, but said Shariah cannot be disregarded to address such issues.
“Review the law further. Consult Islamic scholars and legal experts. Bring necessary amendments. But Shariah cannot be disregarded under any circumstances in the name of resolving a problem,” he said.
Faizul Karim urged the government to conduct a further review of the law and consult Islamic scholars and legal experts before making necessary amendments.
During the question-and-answer session, he said: “I follow Shariah, and you must ensure that I have the opportunity to follow Shariah.”
Asked about women journalists attending IAB programs, he said: “They should come observing purdah.”
On participating in talk shows with women journalists, he said: “If it goes against Shariah, it is not right.”
Elaborating on women’s participation in journalism, Faizul Karim said: “If any of my sisters come, they should come in accordance with Shariah. We are not stopping them. If any of my sisters works as a journalist, we are not stopping her. I am saying this beforehand: Shariah is not meant to create problems; it is meant to solve problems. If my sister works as a journalist, she will do so; but in accordance with Shariah.”
Faizul Karim also alleged that the government was focusing on enacting laws that go against Shariah instead of addressing problems such as rising commodity prices, unemployment, gas and power shortages, extortion and traffic congestion.
He said the situation was disappointing.

item.title: Speakers call for repeal of law criminalizing suicide attempts
item.description:
Mental health experts and activists on Thursday called for repealing the colonial-era law criminalizing attempted suicide at a gathering and candlelight vigil at TSC on the University of Dhaka campus to mark World Suicide Prevention Day.
The event, themed “Changing the Conversation, Strengthening Prevention, Saving Lives,” was organized by the Innovation for Wellbeing Foundation (IWF), the Student Guidance Office of TSC, and the Nasirullah Psychotherapy Unit of the Department of Clinical Psychology at Dhaka University.
Citing police records, organizers said 76,361 people died by suicide in Bangladesh between 2020 and 2024, while another 13,491 died between January and November 2025.
Media-identified cases showed that 513 students died by suicide in 2023, 310 in 2024 and 403 in 2025. At least 10 student suicides were reported nationwide after the 2026 SSC results were published on August 10, although organizers cautioned that the media-based figure is incomplete.
Speakers repeatedly pointed to Section 309 of the Penal Code, 1860, which remains in force and provides for up to one year in prison, a fine, or both for attempted suicide.
Kamal Uddin Ahmed Chowdhury, a professor at Dhaka University’s Department of Clinical Psychology, said the law criminalizes people already in deep distress and called for suicide-prevention centers in all 503 upazilas.
Imdadul Haque Talukdar, a public mental health specialist, also urged reform of the law, highlighting its colonial origins.
He cited WHO estimates showing that Bangladeshi households bear the large majority of healthcare costs out of pocket and pointed to New Zealand’s “wellbeing budget” as a model for prioritizing mental health spending.
Ahommed Takbir Araf, coordinator of TeenTeen, a youth helpline, said 70% to 80% of mental health conditions emerge between the ages of 13 and 19.
However, parents and teachers often dismiss warning signs as a passing phase, leaving teenagers afraid to speak up for fear of being labeled “mad,” he said.
He said his organization is building a judgment-free platform where teenagers can simply be heard.
Mahmuda Rahman Khan, chief operating officer of the Global Center of Excellence, described Suicide First Aid, an international training program that teaches laypeople to assess suicide risk using a framework she called CPR: current plan, previous attempts and resources.
Drawing on her own experience with postpartum depression, she said people rarely announce suicidal intent directly but often signal it indirectly.
“No one who attempts suicide truly wants to die,” she said. “They cannot see a way out of the problem consuming them.”
Organizers called on the government, institutions, health professionals, media and families to strengthen suicide-prevention strategies, support pathways, responsible reporting and open conversations, linking the effort to SDG target 3.4.
The event ended with a candlelight vigil.

item.title: Most child abuse reports on Awaz.bd involve known perpetrators
item.description:
Most people accused of childhood sexual abuse in 132 anonymous reports submitted to Bangladeshi platform Awaz.bd were known to the children, with acquaintances, trusted acquaintances and relatives making up a significant share of the reported perpetrators.
The data also shows that abuse frequently occurred in places where children were expected to be safe, with homes accounting for 48% of the reported incidents and religious or educational institutions for another 35%.
Among male survivors, acquaintances were identified as alleged perpetrators in 37% of cases, followed by trusted acquaintances at 21%, close relatives at 9% and distant relatives at 9%. Strangers accounted for 12%.
For female survivors, distant relatives were the most commonly reported perpetrators at 30%, followed by acquaintances and close relatives at 17% each and trusted acquaintances at 13%.
The findings are based on anonymous submissions to Awaz.bd, a data and awareness platform that documents experiences of childhood sexual abuse. The platform says it is not a helpline or legal assistance service.
According to the data, 10-12-year-olds accounted for 32 reports, while 7-9-year-olds accounted for 20.
Of the reported locations, open spaces accounted for 10% and commercial or transport-related places for 8%.
Religious and educational institutions emerged as another major setting for abuse. Within this category, Qawmi madrasas accounted for 23 reports, or half of all reports involving such institutions. Schools accounted for eight, mosques seven, universities and Alia madrasas three each, and colleges and temples one each. No reports were recorded from pagodas.
The data also indicates that abuse was often not an isolated experience. About 48% of survivors reported multiple incidents, while 15% described abuse that continued over a long period. Another 36% reported a one-time incident.
In 35% of reports, the abuse involved an alleged misuse of power or authority. Another 24% said the abuse began with force and continued through fear, while circumstances were unclear in 39% of cases.
Awaz.bd was founded by Rakibul Hasan and Salahuddin Jahangir. Rakibul, who studied International Relations at the University of Dhaka, said the initiative grew out of concern over child sexual abuse, particularly cases involving boys in madrasa settings.
He said the founders initially intended to document abuse against boys in madrasas, but submissions soon came from both male and female survivors and from different types of educational institutions.
“This is not a help centre or a legal assistance centre. It is an awareness platform,” Rakibul said.
He said the platform was created to document experiences that often remain unreported because of fear, social consequences and the lack of safe avenues for speaking out.
The anonymous accounts submitted to the platform describe alleged abuse by relatives, classmates, neighbors, senior students and other people known to the survivors. Some contributors said they never told anyone about the abuse because they were afraid, confused or unable to speak about what had happened.
Several accounts also describe lasting emotional effects, including fear, shame, trauma and difficulty discussing childhood experiences.
The submissions came from districts across Bangladesh. Dhaka accounted for 28 reports, followed by Chittagong with 11, Cumilla with eight, Noakhali with seven, Narayanganj with six, and Gazipur and Mymensingh with five each.
Rakibul said the founders hope the platform will draw greater attention from the government and madrasa authorities to child safety and create public pressure for stronger action against abuse.
Awaz.bd says it does not ask contributors for their names, photographs or other identifying information. It also says it does not use cookies or tracking tools and does not retain personal information.
However, the 132 submissions should not be interpreted as a national prevalence estimate. The data comes from voluntary anonymous submissions, is not nationally representative and has not been independently verified.
People seeking immediate help can contact Child Helpline 1098, the Women and Children Violence Prevention Helpline at 109, or National Emergency Service 999.

item.title: Barvida demands lifting import ban on reconditioned EVs
item.description:
The Bangladesh Reconditioned Vehicles Importers and Dealers Association (Barvida) has reacted to the ban on importing reconditioned electric vehicles (EVs) in the latest import policy, alleging a quarter has misguided the government despite an agreement reached with them before.
Demanding a withdrawal of the ban at a press conference at Dhaka Club on Wednesday, Barvida leaders said the Import Policy Order 2026-2029 published on August 24 banned the import of reconditioned or used EVs, though it was allowed in the previous policy.
"All of a sudden, the ban has been imposed on us," Barvida president Abdul Haque told the press conference.
Barvida secretary general Reaz Rahman, former presidents, and secretary generals, including Abdul Mannan Khasru, Mahmudul Haq Babul, Shahidul Islam, and Saiful Islam Samrat, spoke on the occasion, among others.
Haque said it was agreed at the discussion level to allow seven-year-old reconditioned EVs, even though Barvida showed all grounds and information for a 10-year limit due to higher standards and quality Japanese EVs than other manufacturing countries.
He said though Barvida members played a visible role in creating the market of automobiles during all technological shifts from VVT-1 to hybrid and plug-in hybrid technology, they had been deprived again like facing discrimination several times in some previous policies.
This ban would also deprive buyers of getting affordable and quality vehicles, as well as impact the economy, Haque further said.
During the press conference, Barvida said the UK allows importing up to 10-year-old EVs, while compliant countries like New Zealand import on some conditions.
Some 29,349 units of reconditioned EVs were exported to 71 countries in 2025 with proper inspection, battery health certification, and safety standards, with Sri Lanka topping the list.
New Zealand and Sri Lanka imported 4,512 units of reconditioned vehicles from Japan last year, with New Zealand importing 3,743.
Bangladesh ranked 24th with 92 units.
Terming the Japanese used EVs greener, high-quality, reliable, and affordable, the BARVIDA president demanded reinstating the provision for importing reconditioned EVs by setting international standards, control, and condition and considering safety, environment-friendliness, certain age, and technical capacity.
As the automobile industry grows centring imports, using and servicing of vehicles, spare parts, technical expertise, assembly and continuation of production, and reconditioned EVs bridge the gap in industrial expansion, Barvida leaders said.
Former Barvida president Khasru blamed brand new EV importers for misguiding policymakers to ban the import of reconditioned EVs, though Japan has already proved itself as a trusted country for high-quality, reliable, and affordable EVs.
They said the battery capacity of Japanese reconditioned vehicles remains at 70% to 80% after use of nearly 200,000 kilometres over 10 to 15 years.

item.title: Home minister: Govt adopts strategic plans to further improve law and order
item.description:
Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed on Thursday said the government has adopted short-, medium- and long-term strategic plans to further improve the country’s law-and-order situation, saying visible progress since the present government took office.
Replying to a question from Chapainawabganj-3 MP Md Nurul Islam during the question-answer session in parliament, he said maintaining overall law and order and ensuring the safety of people and their property are among the government’s highest priorities.
The minister said the police have intensified efforts to prevent murder, mugging, abduction and other forms of crime.
“Efforts are underway to restore the morale of the police force after it was left in a fragile state following the July uprising and make it capable of operating at full strength,” he said.
Salahuddin said further visible improvement in law and order could be achieved quickly with the cooperation of the people, in line with the strategic plans adopted by the government.
Replying to a question from Gaibandha-5 MP Md Abdul Wares, he said 6,286 members of the then Bangladesh Rifles (BDR) were dismissed and 2,510 were sent into compulsory retirement following the 2009 BDR mutiny and brutal killings.
The minister said disciplinary measures and punishments were imposed following legal procedures and no innocent BDR member was dismissed.
As a result, there is no scope for reinstating those who were dismissed, he said, adding that dismissed BDR members who were accused in murder and explosives cases also cannot be reinstated.
Replying to a question from Dhaka-5 MP Mohammed Kamal Hossain, Salahuddin said a project titled “Development of Smart Policing in DMP” has been included in the list of new, unapproved projects under the Annual Development Program (ADP) to bring Dhaka city under a CCTV monitoring system.
He said the project’s Development Project Proposal (DPP) is currently being revised in line with the decision of a scrutiny committee meeting held on the original DPP.
If the project is approved by the Executive Committee of the National Economic Council (ECNEC), necessary steps can be taken to bring the entire Dhaka Metropolitan Police area under a CCTV monitoring system, the minister added.
In reply to a question from reserved-seat MP Salina Sultana, he said 60,598 anti-drug drives were conducted across the country between February 17 and August 31, 2026.
A total of 18,040 cases were filed during the drives, and 18,858 suspected drug traffickers were arrested and brought under the law, Salahuddin said.
Replying to a question from Rajshahi-4 MP Md Abdul Bari Sarder, he said Bangladesh Road Transport Authority (BRTA) data showed that 829 double-decker buses have valid permission to operate on various highways across the country.
However, some unscrupulous bus owners subsequently modified the bodies of double-decker buses and converted them into double-decker sleeper buses for operation on highways, the minister said.
The authorities have cancelled the registrations of several such double-decker sleeper buses through mobile courts, he added.

item.title: Transport workers block road in Mohakhali, disrupt traffic
item.description:
Transport workers blocked a road in Mohakhali in the capital on Thursday afternoon, bringing traffic to a halt in the area.
The workers blocked the road in the Mohakhali Bus Terminal area after 4:30pm, disrupting traffic movement on both sides of the road.
The Traffic Gulshan Division of Dhaka Metropolitan Police (DMP) said buses had been parked on the road in the terminal area in the afternoon, affecting normal traffic movement.
Protesting the move, transport workers blocked the road and took up position there, it said.
As a result, traffic on both sides of the road came to a halt, causing congestion in the area.
Police personnel were at the scene and taking necessary measures to restore normal traffic movement, the DMP said.
The Traffic Gulshan Division of DMP requested city residents to avoid the road adjacent to Mohakhali Bus Terminal and use alternative routes.

item.title: Three confess in Savar SI killing case, two placed on 5-day remand
item.description:
Three accused in a case over the beating death of Special Branch (SB) Sub-Inspector Altaf Hossain at Aminbazar in Dhaka have given confessional statements before a court, while two others have been placed on five-day remand.
The three, Jahurul, Apon and Jihad, gave their confessional statements on Thursday.
Investigation Officer of the case and SI Md Zakir Al-Ahsan of the Aminbazar Police Camp under Savar Model Police Station produced the accused before the court and sought to have their statements recorded after they agreed to confess.
Senior Judicial Magistrate Tajul Islam Sohag recorded the statements of Jahurul and Apon, while Judicial Magistrate Tanvir Ahmed recorded Jihad’s statement. The court subsequently ordered them to be sent to jail.
Meanwhile, Senior Judicial Magistrate Ayesha Siddika placed Kashem Ali and Dadi Al Faiyet Jit on five-day remand for questioning.
Police arrested Kashem from the Baratali Sagarna area of Moulvibazar Sadar around 4:30pm on Tuesday and Jit from the Amratali area under Comilla Sadar Police Station.
They were produced before the court on Wednesday, when police sought 10-day remand. The court sent them to jail and fixed Thursday for the remand hearing.
Assistant Sub-Inspector Abu Bakkar Siddique said defence lawyers sought cancellation of the remand and bail for the accused, while the prosecution sought the maximum remand. After hearing both sides, the court granted five-day remand.
On Tuesday, the court granted five-day remand for Md Alauddin, 29, Md Apon, 26, Md Jihad, 23, Imran Hossain, 25, Nur Mohammad Rudra, 24, and Md Golam Rabbi, 22. Billal, 34, and Delwar, 33, were placed on three-day remand.
Earlier, Jahurul, the prime accused, was placed on five-day remand on Monday, while Rakib Mia, Sabbir Ahmed and Wasim were placed on three-day remand on Wednesday.
According to the case statement, an altercation broke out around 7:30pm on September 5 over the parking of an auto-rickshaw in front of Abul Kalam Azad’s garage in West Baradevi, Savar.
Altaf Hossain tried to intervene but came under attack. He took shelter at his son Ariful Islam’s business establishment, Grand Fashion.
Around 8:10pm, the accused allegedly attacked Altaf with locally made weapons, beating him indiscriminately with rods, pipes, hammers and sticks and leaving him critically injured.
When Ariful tried to rescue his father, the attackers allegedly hacked him with sharp weapons.
The accused also allegedly vandalised the business establishment, causing damage worth Tk5 lakh, and took away Tk2.20 lakh in cash, according to the case statement.

item.title: 336 students pass after SSC result re-scrutiny in Comilla
item.description:
A total of 1,944 students under the Comilla Education Board have had their SSC results changed following a re-scrutiny of their answer scripts for the 2026 examinations.
Of them, 1,608 students saw changes in their grades, while a total of 207 students achieved GPA-5. Another 336 students who initially failed were declared passed.
The re-scrutiny results were published on Thursday through a notice signed by Papia Akter, deputy controller of examinations at the Comilla Education Board.
Board Chairman Prof Md Ahsan Parvez said experienced teachers were involved in the re-scrutiny process. “We assigned experienced teachers to conduct the re-scrutiny. The answer scripts for which applications were submitted were thoroughly examined in accordance with the relevant rules before the revised results were published,” he said. “We are pleased with the changes in the students’ results,” he added.
According to the board data, 145,839 students appeared in the 2026 SSC examinations under the Comilla Board. A total of 35,929 students applied online for re-scrutiny of 91,494 answer scripts in different subjects.
However, 211 students could not secure a passing grade despite changes in their marks. Students whose results have changed following the re-scrutiny will be able to apply online for college admission on September 12 and 13, Prof Ahsan Parvez said.

item.title: Sundarbans regains vibrancy after three-month closure
item.description:
The Sundarbans has regained its vibrancy after a three-month closure, with thousands of fishermen returning to its rivers and canals and tourists once again flocking to the world’s largest mangrove forest.
The 91-day ban on the entry of tourists and forest-dependent communities, imposed to protect biodiversity and ensure the breeding of wildlife and aquatic species, ended on August 31. The forest was reopened on September 1.
In the first six days after reopening, 36 tourist launches carrying 2,520 visitors, including eight foreign nationals, entered the Sundarbans, according to Forest Department officials. During the same period, 5,844 boats received boat licence certificates (BLCs) to enter the forest for fishing and crab collection.
The Sundarbans has 14 designated tourist spots under its eastern and western forest divisions. Every year, several lakh tourists visit the forest, while thousands of forest-dependent people enter with permission to collect fish, crabs, golpata and honey.
Since 2021, Forest Department has imposed the annual closure during the breeding season to minimize human disturbance and protect the forest’s biodiversity.
The reopening has already brought renewed activity to popular tourist destinations, particularly Karamjal in Bagerhat. Tourist vessels are regularly arriving at the jetty, while visitors are exploring foot trails and travelling to destinations, including Katka, Kochikhali, Jamtala and Andharmanik.
Visitors are arriving with family members, friends and organised groups to experience the forest’s rivers, canals and wildlife. Many are seen taking photographs and videos of deer, monkeys and other animals.
Karamjal Wildlife Breeding Centre officer-in-charge Hawlader Azad Kabir said tourist numbers were initially lower due to adverse weather but had been increasing as conditions improved. “We have taken necessary measures to ensure that tourists can visit safely and comfortably,” he said, urging visitors to act responsibly to help protect the fragile ecosystem.
Sundarbans East Division Divisional Forest Officer Md Rezaul Karim Chowdhury said the three-month closure had produced visible benefits for the forest and its wildlife. “During the closure, we observed a significant increase in the presence of fish in different canals. Wildlife also moved more freely,” he said.
He added that large herds of deer and tigers had been spotted during the closure, while several wildlife sightings were captured by Forest Department personnel.
Forest officials said the closure allowed wildlife to move with fewer disturbances. Tigers, crocodiles, deer, wild boars and monkeys were seen at different locations during the three-month period.
Sharankhola Range Assistant Conservator of Forests Md Shariful Islam said surveillance and patrols had been strengthened during the closure to prevent forest crimes and illegal entry. “Smart patrols were conducted for 20 days a month instead of the usual seven days, while patrol teams remained active round the clock depending on the tides,” he said.
Forest officials believe the return of tourists and fishermen, alongside increased sightings of wildlife and fish, reflects the positive impact of the three-month closure on the Sundarbans ecosystem.

item.title: Floating rafts open new prospects for mussel, coral fish farming in Cox’s Bazar
item.description:
Floating rafts have opened up new opportunities for green mussel and high-value coral fish farming in Cox’s Bazar, offering coastal communities an alternative source of income while creating fresh prospects for the country’s blue economy.
An experimental farm has been established near the mouth of the Bakkhali River in Sadar upazila of Cox’s Bazar, where local farmers are cultivating green mussels and coral fish using simple and environment-friendly technology.
The floating structures are made of bamboo, ropes and plastic drums. Mussel seeds are suspended beneath the rafts, allowing them to grow naturally in saline water. The mussels benefit from tidal flows and favorable coastal conditions, requiring little additional technology.
Project officials said mussels generally become suitable for harvesting within a few months. With demand for nutritious marine food increasing in Bangladesh, they believe commercial-scale production could meet domestic demand and eventually create opportunities for exports.
At the same time, high-value coral fish are being raised in large net cages attached to floating rafts. Fish fry is released into the cages and reared with regular feeding and care until they reach marketable size.
As coral fish fetch relatively high prices in local markets, farmers see considerable potential for generating profits from the venture.
Anwar Mia, a green mussel farmer, said he began cultivating green mussels on floating rafts in 2018 and has since been making profits from the initiative. “Floating mussel farming has been successful and has created an additional source of income alongside fishing,” he said.
He said such farms could become particularly important during periods when fishermen are unable to go to sea because of bad weather or seasonal fishing bans.
Another farmer, Shahidul Islam Babu, said fishing had previously been their main source of income. “When bad weather struck or fishing was banned, our income stopped. Now we are earning regularly by farming mussels and coral fish on floating rafts,” he said.
“With proper training and government support, this farming can be expanded on a larger scale,” he added.
Local farmer Mong Chen said he was initially hesitant about adopting the new technology but gained confidence after receiving training and technical assistance from the Integrated Development Foundation (IDF).
“The market price is good, and our family’s financial condition has improved. If farmers receive loans on easier terms and support with marketing, many more entrepreneurs will become interested in this sector,” he said.
The project is funded by Palli Karma-Sahayak Foundation (PKSF) and implemented by Integrated Development Foundation (IDF). It provides local farmers with training, technical assistance and capacity-building support on modern marine aquaculture techniques.
Mohammad Hasan, an IDF fisheries officer, said the prospects for green mussel and marine fish farming on floating rafts in Bangladesh were very promising. “Coastal areas have abundant saline water and favorable environmental conditions, allowing the sector to expand rapidly,” he said.
Hasan said coordinated support from the government, research institutions and private organisations could turn floating aquaculture into a profitable and sustainable livelihood for coastal communities.
He said the initiative could also contribute to Bangladesh’s blue economy by making better use of the country’s extensive coastline and marine resources. “It can contribute to food security, create employment and generate foreign exchange,” he said.

item.title: Global drug policy body urges protection for children caught in drug economies
item.description:
The Global Commission on Drug Policy has urged governments to move away from punitive drug policies and recognize children and young people involved in illicit drug economies as victims in need of protection, healthcare and support.
Launching a new policy brief in Geneva on Wednesday, the commission said children and young people are profoundly affected by drug laws and their enforcement, regardless of whether they use drugs themselves. Their rights, experiences and voices, however, remain largely absent from drug policy discussions.
The brief, titled Making Children and Young People Visible in Drug Policy: A Child Rights-Based Agenda for Reform , calls for policies based on evidence, public health, human rights, child protection and meaningful participation by young people.
“Children are too often invoked to justify punitive drug policies, while the harms those policies cause them remain invisible,” said Helen Clark, chair of the commission and former prime minister of New Zealand.
“A policy cannot be called protective if it criminalizes children, separates families, denies them healthcare, and/or punishes those who have been exploited,” she said.
The commission said punitive approaches can expose children to arrest, detention and violence, while separating them from their families, disrupting education and limiting access to essential medicines and health services.
It called for children and young people recruited or exploited within illicit drug economies to be treated primarily as victims rather than offenders.
Poverty, violence, displacement and exclusion can create conditions for organized criminal groups to exploit children, the commission said. Child protection, education, social protection and community-based support should therefore take precedence over punishment, which can deepen their vulnerability.
“Children involved in illicit drug economies are often trying to survive in conditions shaped by poverty, violence, and exclusion,” said Juan Manuel Santos, a commission member, former president of Colombia and Nobel laureate.
“Treating them as criminals compounds the exploitation they have already experienced,” he said, calling on governments to hold accountable those who recruit and profit from children while providing them with protection, education and safe routes out.
The commission identified four priorities: preventing the detention of children under punitive drug policies; ensuring access to essential controlled medicines; providing child- and youth-friendly health services; and protecting children exploited in illicit drug economies.
It urged governments to expand diversion, restorative justice and community-based alternatives for children arrested or prosecuted for drug use, possession or involvement in illicit drug economies.
It also called for equitable access to medicines needed for pain relief and palliative care, noting that regulatory barriers, weak health systems and inadequate pediatric formulations can leave children without essential treatment.
For young people facing drug-related harms, the commission recommended confidential, evidence-based and youth-friendly health services.
It said stigma, age restrictions and barriers to confidential care can prevent young people from receiving timely support.
Harm-reduction measures, including access to naloxone and other overdose-prevention interventions, should form part of a broader continuum of prevention, treatment, recovery, mental health and social support, it said.
The commission said children remain largely overlooked in international drug policymaking.
Between 2000 and 2026, the UN Commission on Narcotic Drugs adopted approximately 300 resolutions, but only 19 specifically focused on children and young people.
The new brief drew on 11 consultations across five continents involving more than 150 participants from about 47 countries, including children and young people, child rights advocates, health professionals, civil society organizations, government representatives, UN officials and drug policy experts.
“Policies talk about youth, but youth are never part of the discussion. We want to be part of the solution, but no one invites us to the table,” a young participant from Pakistan said.
The commission urged governments and UN entities to allocate resources equitably to communities disproportionately affected by drug policies and related harms.
The brief comes as the international drug control system undergoes a review mandated by the UN Commission on Narcotic Drugs in March 2025.
The commission said the process offers an opportunity to give children and young people a greater role in shaping future drug policy.
A child- and youth-friendly version of the brief has also been released.
The Global Commission on Drug Policy comprises 26 commissioners, including 15 former heads of state and government and leaders from politics, public health, human rights, law enforcement, civil society and academia.
It promotes evidence-based drug policies grounded in public health, human rights and social justice.

item.title: Fire on cargo ship in China kills 20 people
item.description:
A fire erupted Thursday on a foreign-flagged cargo ship docked in an Chinese port, leaving at least 20 people dead and five missing, state media said.
The bulk carrier, moored in the eastern shipping hub of Qingdao, had 42 people on board when the fire broke out, according to state broadcaster CCTV.
Of those, 17 have been evacuated including five who were injured, and another five were still missing. Twenty people were found with “no signs of life,” CCTV said.
The broadcaster said that “the open flames were extinguished at around 2:30 pm (0630 GMT).” State news agency Xinhua earlier said that the fire broke out at around 11:15 am.
“A foreign cargo ship of Beihai Shipbuilding Co., Ltd. in Qingdao, Shandong Province, caught fire during its port call for maintenance, causing heavy casualties,” Xinhua said, without specifying the cause of the fire.
President Xi Jinping called for urgent search and rescue operations, and “stressed the need to... strictly hold those responsible to account,” Xinhua said.
A witness from a neighboring residential compound told AFP he saw thick smoke coming from the ship, but did not hear an explosion.
“I saw the smoke from the ship by chance, but there was no visible fire,” he said.
“I didn’t hear an explosion or smell anything.”
Xinhua shared a photo of the scene showing a large ship called the Ocean Melody docked at a yard, with several fire trucks stationed in front of it.
Ocean Melody is a 190-metre (623-foot) long bulk carrier sailing under the Liberian flag, according to vessel tracking website MarineTraffic, which located the ship as moored in Qingdao.
Qingdao is the hometown and namesake of Tsingtao beer and a major international maritime hub, connected to more than 700 ports in over 180 countries and regions, according to state media.
The Qingdao Beihai Shipbuilding yard operates as a subsidiary of the China State Shipbuilding Corporation.
Xi said that “all regions and relevant departments must draw profound lessons from this incident, thoroughly investigate and rectify all types of fire hazards.”
There have been several major industrial accidents in China over the last year, where safety regulations are often lax.
In August, an explosion and ensuing fire at a shipyard in Fujian province killed one fire and rescue worker, and injured 12 others, according to state media.
China launched a campaign against fire hazards in high-rise buildings last November, after a huge blaze engulfed several tower blocks in Hong Kong, killing 168 people.
In May, a blast at a fireworks factory in central China killed 37 people, marking one of the nation’s deadliest industrial accidents in years.
And a fire in a shoe factory in eastern Fujian province in July killed at least 28 people.

item.title: ULAB hosts freshers’ orientation for Fall 2026

item.title: Dr Shahnewaz leads Bangladesh team at APSCO CubeSat camp
item.description:
Bangladeshi researcher Dr Shahnewaz Siddique of the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering at North South University (NSU) led a research team at the APSCO CubeSat Competition (ACC) Summer Camp in Xi’an, China, from August 12 to 25, 2026.
Organized under the Asia-Pacific Space Cooperation Organization (APSCO), the camp provided hands-on training in key CubeSat subsystems, including onboard computing, control, communications, power, structural integration, thermal management, and ground-station interfacing.
The training was held at Northwestern Polytechnical University, a leading Chinese university.
Dr Shahnewaz’s team qualified for the camp through a rigorous selection process coordinated by the Bangladesh Space Research and Remote Sensing Organization (SPARRSO), Bangladesh’s focal agency for APSCO.
Following SPARRSO’s call for participation, the team submitted detailed CubeSat designs, which were evaluated and approved by an APSCO expert panel.
The team will now move to the next phase of the project: building, testing, and validating the engineering model of the proposed CubeSat.
The development marks a significant step towards advancing CubeSat and space-technology research in Bangladesh.

item.title: Why does Pather Panchali still call us
item.description:
Before Apu understands the vastness of the world, he begins to learn how little of it can be kept.
Apu wanders through fields and along village paths, listening to stories and following his sister Durga, who discovers riches in places adults have stopped noticing. Then, beyond the white kash fields, a train appears on the horizon. To the children, it is a marvel. To the reader, it is something more: a sign that childhood and innocence will not last forever after all; they will be ploughed under the cruel reality.
Almost a hundred years after its publication, Pather Panchalistill finds its readers' minds tugging at the moment when awe collides with despair. Childhood unfolds within poverty, affection exists without security, and every promise of departure carries the possibility of loss.
Whereas a childhood built from small things.
Bibhutibhushan Bandopadhyay’s novel draws interesting moments from seemingly insignificant things; perhaps that is why it becomes so interesting. No royalty, no battle, and no victory. Instead, we will find ponds soaking in sunshine, bamboo groves that hum in the wind, an old woman who spins tales, and two kids who meander wherever they go.
This world has the spirit of Durga. She sneaks into orchards looking for fruits, roams villages barefoot, and finds treasure in places where adults see nothing at all. She is combated by poverty but will not allow her wonder to be taken.
Bandopadhyay sees what many writers fail to: childhood is not about stuff, but fresh joy. For Durga, a guava snatched from the orchard may be like mining gold from a mine.
Alas! Even in this blissful background, poverty leaves its mark as darkness appears when the lights are off: you can’t escape from it.
The conflict between poverty and a child’s innocence goes beyond when neighbors accuse Durga of stealing fruit. The allegation puts a family's dignity on the brink. In this scene, the author captures a reality common to many South Asian households: how adults care about being seen as honorable or not and how adults are worried about the scarcity of resources, while children just want to taste the sweet flavors in life.
The village is never just a setting. It exists and breathes with the characters.
That’s why the ponds, fields, mango trees, riverbanks, and bamboo groves create the landscape of Apu's boundless imagination and exploration. Before he learns from books, he learns from clouds, sounds, stories, and seasons.
One of the novel's most memorable figures, Indir Thakrun, belongs to this world as completely as the frail, poor, and often unwanted. Through Indir Thakrun, Bandopadhyay explores the frailty of old age. Even though she is cherished for her humor, narrative personality, and presence, she seldom gets the safety and validation she requires. Even her solitude reflects a terrible social truth we face every day—love is not enough. It cannot compensate for a lack of safety, housing, or kindness from humans.
Then comes the monsoon.
The monsoon initially appears as liberation. Durga runs into the rain with unrestrained delight. For a brief time, poverty seems to recede as the storm dissolves the boundaries imposed by property, accusation, and scarcity.
However, Bandopadhyay allows no separation of beauty from vulnerability. Wonder comes with the monsoon, but it also brings along an unseen danger. The rain that animates the countryside also exposes the weakness of the family’s shelter and the vulnerability of Durga’s body. Nature in Pather Panchali is neither vicious nor gracious, and it does not even deign to reminisce over man's wish. It gives life and heals; it destroys and survives. This delicate tension between beauty and peril provides the emotional heft of most of the novel.
The great turning point of the novel arrives with Durga's death.
There are a few scenes in Bengali literature that leave the reader feeling even more devastated when Durga dies. Because Bandopadhyay avoids melodrama. Instead of emphasizing death itself, he emphasizes absence.
The laughter fades. The companionship fades. The silence remains.
The ponds continue reflecting the sky. The bamboo still moves in the wind. The paths accept other footsteps. This continuity deepens Apu’s grief because the landscape he shared with Durga survives without her.
Memory preserves her presence, but it cannot restore her. Familiar places now carry incompatible meanings: they contain both the joy of what happened and the pain of what cannot happen again.
Apu gains knowledge from this loss, but that knowledge is not compensation. To describe his suffering simply as a step toward maturity would make Durga’s death seem useful. His world becomes larger and poorer at once.
The train beyond the kash fields once represented discovery. After Durga’s death, movement also means separation. Any road leading Apu forward must now lead him away from someone who cannot follow.
Perhaps the most heartbreaking scene occurs later.
Harihar comes home after so long, bringing gifts for his family. Some of the presents are meant for Durga. He speaks excitedly, imagining her happiness.
But Durga is gone.
The gift remains an expression of love, yet its meaning has changed. Harihar left to improve the family’s circumstances, but his absence prevented him from witnessing the event that transformed them. What he brings cannot repair what happened while he was away.
This scene is wrenching because of its simplicity. No big words and no surprise. There is no grand speech and no dramatic revelation. A father carrying gifts for a daughter who will never receive them is enough to break the heart of the readers.
Bandopadhyay has more faith in ordinary human feeling than in theater tragedy, and that faith pays off for the reader.
The insight into ordinary humanity is what makes Pather Panchali timeless.
Though readers have changed since the days of smartphones, algorithms, and constant flows of information, the feelings that ran through this novel are still relevant. People continue to be displaced in pursuit of opportunity. Families still live under economic pressure. Childhood still ends too quickly. And Memory still becomes a sort of space where the losses are living there.
It is images, not arguments that survive past the last page: Durga running through an orchard, Indir Thakrun telling tales, a father arriving home late, and a train passing beyond the kash fields. There is something timeless and universal about these pictures: they tap into a human need to belong, remember, and move on despite loss.
Some writers leave behind books. Bibhutibhushan Bandopadhyay has left a world. On his birthday, we remember that the author may be no more, but Apu still runs into fields, and Durga reaches toward what is beyond her grasp, and a train emerges from the sea of kash flowers with the promise of a new life on board. In the course of this novel, Bandopadhyay also implies that there is no ending to a road in life. It takes us away from home while teaching us to take the home in ourselves. And this concept loops through generations of readers. It is not just existence but literary survival. It is some sort of immortality.
Many years later this whistle can still be heard after the last page has been turned. It echoes not just from the world of Apu but also our memories: love, loss, and becoming. This is the reason why the road of Pather Panchali continues to call you.
Anik Karmakar is an MA in English Literature graduate from Visva-Bharati University, India.

item.title: Bank sub-branches lead in deposits, lag in disbursing loans
item.description:
Along with keeping urban activity operational, banks in the country are now turning toward rural areas as well.
However, instead of opening full-fledged branches at higher costs, banks are rapidly expanding financial services by relying on low-cost, small-scale sub-branches.
This alternative strategy for collecting local deposits is yielding positive results.
On one hand, it has made it easier to bring banking services to remote areas; on the other hand, driven by the remarkable activity of these sub-branches, the number of clients, bank accounts, and local deposit volume are surging overnight.
However, there is a stark contradiction to this positive trend.
Although local deposit collection has grown rapidly, investments are primarily centralized in main offices and major branches.
As a result, only a nominal fraction of the collected local deposits is being disbursed locally as loans.
This picture emerged from the latest updated report of Bangladesh Bank.
According to data from Bangladesh Bank for the June quarter of this year, deposits collected from these sub-branches increased by Tk4,546 crore in three months compared to March.
Deposits rose from Tk79,717 crore in March to Tk84,263 crore in June—representing a deposit growth rate of 5.7%.
In contrast, deposits across the overall banking sector grew by just 2.4% during the same period.
This indicates that the rate of deposit growth in sub-branches is nearly 2.5 times faster than the banking sector's average.
Beyond the monetary volume, the customer base is also expanding rapidly.
Deposit accounts in sub-branches stood at 8.47 million in March, rising to 8.97 million in June.
Nearly 500,000 new accounts were added in three months.
Consequently, the share of sub-branches in total bank deposits increased from 3.7% to 3.8%.
Rurals lead the way
A major portion of this expansion came from rural areas.
The rural share of total sub-branch deposits rose from 32.8% in March to 33.9% in June.
The share of female deposit accounts also ticked up from 38.2% to 38.4%, highlighting the growing role of sub-branches in collecting small savings directly from communities.
However, that success has not translated into lending. Loans and advances extended by sub-branches stood at Tk22,309 crore in March, which fell to Tk20,602 crore in June—a decline of Tk1,707 crore or 7.7%.
During the same period, loans and advances across the entire banking sector grew by 1.4%.
Sub-branch loans now account for a mere 1.1% of total bank credit.
Bangladesh Bank executive director and spokesperson Arief Hossain Khan said that due to relatively lower operational costs, banks are now focusing more on expanding sub-branches rather than setting up full branches.
This enables them to bring the rural population under the umbrella of banking services while keeping bank expenditure relatively low.
The growing count of sub-branches further demonstrates how attractive this low-cost model has become to banks.
The total number of sub-branches increased from 4,992 in March to 5,033 in June—a net addition of 41 sub-branches in three months.
This network expansion involved opening 30 new rural sub-branches and 19 urban ones, while 8 sub-branches were either closed or merged.

item.title: Robi introduces AI Space with multiple AI models under one subscription
item.description:
Robi Axiata PLC has launched Robi AI Space, an all-in-one AI platform integrated into the My Robi app, in Bangladesh on September 9, 2026.
Through a partnership with the platform Every AI, the service gives local users access to artificial intelligence models including ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude and DeepSeek through a single premium subscription or selected AI bundle packs.
With credit card penetration in Bangladesh at 1.6%, international payment barriers have limited access to global digital services. Robi’s offering allows customers to access AI models or purchase AI tokens using local mobile data bundles.
The platform is aimed at students, freelancers and entrepreneurs, offering tools for research, writing, business planning and everyday workflows.
Users can also monitor their live token balances through the Every AI interface, reducing the need for multiple overseas subscriptions or separate payment accounts.
Robi said the launch is the beginning of a broader AI ecosystem that it plans to develop. Alongside Every AI, Robi AI Space is envisioned as a dedicated platform bringing together various AI-powered solutions for local subscribers.
Commenting on the launch, Robi Managing Director and CEO Ziad Shatara said: “With credit card penetration posing a structural hurdle, our market has long faced restricted access to global digital tools. By introducing this all-in-one AI platform through My Robi, we are bridging that divide. It’s a major step toward democratizing advanced digital technologies, lowering adoption barriers, and empowering our youth and wider population to harness world-class AI capabilities seamlessly through local mobile connectivity.”
Robi AI Space is now available to all Robi customers through the Robi AI Space section of the My Robi app.

item.title: BES presents ‘Highlights from ADA 2026’ in Dhaka
item.description:
Bangladesh Endocrine Society (BES) organized “Highlights from ADA 2026” Wednesday at the Grand Ballroom of Pan Pacific Sonargaon, Dhaka.
The daylong scientific program brought together leading endocrinology and diabetes specialists to discuss selected contemporary developments and clinical perspectives from the field.
The program featured five scientific sessions covering a broad range of important topics, including pre-diabetes and diabetes risk prediction, insulin resistance, diabetes technology, diabetes in pregnancy, nutrition, weight management, hypertriglyceridemia, and emerging obesity therapies.
The scientific discussions also addressed diabetic neuropathy, diabetic kidney disease and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), while the final session explored diabetes management across the cancer continuum and Type 5 Diabetes in South Asia.
Eminent endocrinologists from home & abroad shared the latest evidence and guideline-based insights through scientific presentations at the event.
Distinguished speakers included Dr Scott D. Isaacs, adjunct instructor, Emory University School of Medicine, Atlanta, Georgia, US & immediate past president, AACE (2025), Dr Faria Afsana, president, Bangladesh Endocrine Society (BES); Dr Shahjada Selim, president-elect, BES; and Dr M Saifuddin, general secretary, BES, along with other renowned experts and speakers.
ACI DIABETES CARE has served as the exclusive scientific partner of “Highlights from ADA 2026, for all four consecutive years since the program have been started.

item.title: Prime Bank joins BB’s Tk3,000cr refinance scheme to support export-oriented industries
item.description:
Prime Bank PLC has signed a participation agreement with Bangladesh Bank, formally joining the Export Diversification Refinance Scheme as a participating financial institution (PFI).
The agreement will enable Prime Bank to provide its export-oriented clients with access to refinance facilities under the scheme.
The agreement was signed recently by Faisal Rahman, chief executive officer of Prime Bank PLC, and AKM Nurunnobi, director, Sustainable Finance Department, Bangladesh Bank.
Under the scheme, Prime Bank will be eligible to avail refinance facilities to support export-oriented industries operating in priority and special development sectors identified under Bangladesh’s Export Policy 2024-2027.
The refinance scheme is aimed at encouraging exporters to diversify their product offerings and explore new international markets, while enhancing competitiveness and strengthening Bangladesh’s export base beyond traditional sectors.
The participation reinforces Prime Bank’s continued efforts to expand access to sustainable and priority-sector financing for Bangladeshi businesses.
It also further strengthens the bank’s collaboration with Bangladesh Bank in advancing the country’s export diversification agenda and supporting the long-term growth of the export sector.

item.title: Nusraat Faria and Badhan set to star in ‘Lojja’
item.description:
Nusraat Faria and Azmeri Haque Badhan are set to share the screen in the upcoming film “Lojja”, jointly produced by Impress Telefilm and Jaaz Multimedia.
Directed by M H Khokon, the film was officially announced on September 8, coinciding with Faria’s 31st birthday.
A signing ceremony for the project was held at the Channel i office on September 5. Faridur Reza Sagar, managing director of Impress Telefilm Limited and Channel i, and Abdul Aziz, owner of Jaaz Multimedia, attended the event alongside members of the production team.
Aziz has written the story of “Lojja”. According to the producers, filming is scheduled to begin on September 20, with a theatrical release planned for next year. The film will later be released on the OTT platform iScreen.
The makers have yet to disclose details about the story or the characters played by Faria and Badhan. However, Aziz described “Lojja” as a socially conscious film and said the release date has not yet been finalized.
Badhan is known for her work in films including “Rehana Maryam Noor” and “Khufiya”. “Rehana Maryam Noor” premiered in the Un Certain Regard section of the 74th Cannes Film Festival, bringing her international recognition.
Meanwhile, Faria is completing work on her web film “Lapatta”, directed by Mehedi Hassan Hridoy. The project has one song sequence left to film and is scheduled to premiere on iScreen in October.

item.title: Nirvana to receive Video Vanguard Award at 2026 MTV VMAs
item.description:
Rock band Nirvana will receive the Video Vanguard Award at the 2026 MTV Video Music Awards, recognizing the band’s lasting influence on music videos and visual culture.
MTV announced the honor on September 9, exactly 34 years after Nirvana made its first appearance at the VMAs in 1992. The band performed “Lithium” at that ceremony, in a performance that became one of the event’s most notable moments.
Nirvana won five VMAs during its career, including Best New Artist in a Video and Best Alternative Video in 1992. The band gained international recognition with its 1991 album “Nevermind,” followed by “In Utero” in 1993.
Frontman Kurt Cobain died in 1994. The band’s surviving members, Dave Grohl, Krist Novoselic and Pat Smear, have since reunited occasionally for special performances featuring guest vocalists.
In 2014, Grohl, Novoselic and Smear performed Nirvana songs with Joan Jett, Kim Gordon, St Vincent and Lorde during the band’s induction into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame. The surviving members also reunited for the FireAid benefit concert in 2025.
It has not yet been confirmed which members will attend this year’s ceremony or whether the award will be accompanied by a tribute performance.
Previous recipients of the Video Vanguard Award include Mariah Carey, Katy Perry, Shakira, and Nicki Minaj.
The 2026 MTV Video Music Awards will be held in Los Angeles on September 27. The ceremony will air live on CBS and MTV and stream on Paramount+. A host has yet to be announced.

item.title: Nora Fatehi sued for Rs three crore over ‘Lego airplane’ remarks
item.description:
Bollywood actor Nora Fatehi is facing a Rs 3 crore civil defamation suit filed by aviation company Dunes Aviation over remarks she allegedly made about one of its chartered aircraft.
The company filed the suit at a Gandhinagar court, where Senior Civil Judge R Agarwal is scheduled to hear the matter on September 25.
According to the lawsuit, Nora recorded videos aboard a Cessna Citation CJ2 during a Mumbai-Jaipur flight in December last year. She allegedly described the aircraft as “miniature”, a “toy” and a “Lego airplane” before posting the videos on Instagram.
Dunes Aviation has alleged that the remarks were made without technical knowledge or verification and caused damage to its reputation and business. The company claims the posts also contributed to booking cancellations.
The aviation firm further alleged that bookings have declined by 15 to 20% since the remarks, while cancellations have increased. It argued that Nora’s large social media following amplified the impact of her comments.
Dunes Aviation maintained that the aircraft was appropriately sized for the journey and had been certified by India’s Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA). According to the company, the aircraft was airworthy and operating legally under a valid Non-Scheduled Operator’s Permit.
Alongside Rs 3 crore in damages, the company has asked the court to order the removal of social media posts containing the remarks or references to the aircraft.
Dunes Aviation has also sought a public clarification from Nora over the comments.

item.title: Widow’s Bay leads Creative Arts Emmys with eight wins
item.description:
“Widow’s Bay” emerged as the biggest winner on the second night of the 78th Emmy Awards, taking home eight awards at the Creative Arts Emmys in Los Angeles on September 6.
The Apple TV comedy-horror series, set on a New England island, won Outstanding Guest Actress in a Comedy Series for Betty Gilpin, along with awards for casting, production design, sound editing, sound mixing, cinematography, music supervision, and music composition.
“DTF St. Louis” followed with six wins. David Harbour and Linda Cardellini received awards for their supporting performances in the limited or anthology series, while creator Steve Conrad won for writing and directing. The series also picked up awards for picture editing and cinematography.
“Spider-Noir” collected five awards, including Outstanding Cinematography for a Series, Outstanding Stunt Coordination for Comedy Programming, Outstanding Title Design, Outstanding Special Visual Effects in a Single Episode and Outstanding Sound Editing for a Comedy or Drama Series.
Julie Andrews added another Emmy to her career record after winning Outstanding Character Voice-Over Performance for her role as Lady Whistledown in “Bridgerton”. It marked her second consecutive win in the category, following her 2025 victory.
Another notable moment came when Rob Reiner posthumously won Outstanding Guest Actor in a Comedy Series for his role as Albert in “The Bear”. The award marked his third Emmy and first acting win since 1978. He became the first actor to receive a posthumous acting Emmy since Raul Julia in 1995.
Shailene Woodley won Outstanding Guest Actress in a Drama Series for “Paradise”, while Ernest Harden Jr. took Outstanding Guest Actor in a Drama Series for “The Pitt”. “South Park” won Outstanding Animated Program.
“The Pitt” and “Pluribus” each secured four awards, while “Beef”, “Margo’s Got Money Troubles” and “Palm Royale” won three each. “Bridgerton”, “Fallout” and “Genndy Tartakovsky’s Primal” each received two.
The Television Academy also introduced the Legacy Award, with “I Love Lucy” becoming its first recipient. The new honor recognizes television programs that have had a lasting impact on audiences, culture, and the industry.
The Creative Arts Emmy ceremonies held on September 5 and 6 will be edited into a single broadcast on FXX on September 12.
The 78th Primetime Emmy Awards, hosted by Mariska Hargitay, will take place on September 14 at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles.

item.title: Dengue: Six deaths mark second highest daily toll this year
item.description:
Six more people died of dengue in Bangladesh in the 24 hours to Thursday morning, marking the second-highest daily death toll from the mosquito-borne disease this year.
With the latest fatalities, the number of dengue deaths in the country has risen to 139 this year, according to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS).
Of the new deaths, two were reported in Khulna division, while one each was recorded in Barisal, Chittagong, Dhaka and Rajshahi divisions.
Of the deaths recorded this year, 65.7% were men and 34.3% were women.
Earlier on Tuesday, Bangladesh recorded its highest number of dengue deaths in a single day this year, with nine people succumbing to the mosquito-borne disease.
In the latest 24 hours, 1,492 more dengue patients were hospitalized, raising the total number of cases this year to 48,430.
Of them, 44,857 patients have been discharged after recovery, according to the DGHS.
